en: #Indian || Āūṃ ||
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstra.

I bow to the lotus feet of Vighneśvara, the elephant-faced son of Umā, who is served by hosts of spirits and others, who consumes the essence of kapittha and jambu fruits, and who is the cause of the destruction of sorrow.
Chapter One: On the Exposition of the Sequence of Emanation.
Then once, having approached the best of sages, Parāśara, who knows the three divisions of time, Maitreya bowed down with palms joined in reverence and questioned him. || 1 ||
O Blessed One, [I have heard] the supreme merit, the secret, the most excellent limb of the Vedas—the three divisions known as Jyotiṣa, consisting of Horā, Gaṇita, and Saṃhitā. || 2 ||
O Sage, it is heard that among these three as well, the *hora* is the most excellent;
O Lord, I desire to hear about it from you—please tell me out of compassion. (3)
How did this creation come to be, and how does the dissolution of the world occur?
Tell me in detail the connection between those situated in the sky and those situated on the earth.
"Excellent, O Brahmin, you who act for the benefit of the world have asked well!
Now I shall speak again of the Supreme Brahman and its power, Bhāratī."
Having bowed to Sūrya, the lord of the planets and the cause of the world's origin,
I shall explain the calculation of the Vedas as it was heard from the mouth of Brahmā.
It should be given to one who is peaceful, devoted to the guru, always truthful, and a believer; through that, he shall indeed attain the highest good.
It should not be given to the disciple of another, nor to an atheist, nor to a rogue;
if it is given, suffering arises daily—of this there is no doubt.
Viṣṇu alone is the unmanifest self, without beginning, the Lord, the Sovereign;
he is pure being, the Master of the world, devoid of qualities yet endowed with the three qualities.
The illustrious creator of saṃsāra, whose self is the causal sign and who is full of majesty,
creates and protects the entire world with one portion of himself as if in play.
The seers of reality know that three-quarters of it are indeed immortal; they also know its measure, including the primary elements, as being one-quarter.
Viṣṇu, who consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, is indeed celebrated as Vāsudeva;
for Viṣṇu, in his unmanifest nature, is endowed with these two powers.
Manifest in nature and endowed with the three qualities, He is said to possess infinite power.
Śrī-Śakti is characterized by the quality of Sattva, while Bhū-Śakti is characterized by the quality of Rajas.
The third power, which was previously mentioned as named Nīla and having the form of darkness, became Vāsudeva when impelled by the power of Śrī. 14.
He assumes the forms of Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
endowed with the power of tamas, the god Viṣṇu is named Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Pradyumna is endowed with passion (rajas) and power (śakti), while Aniruddha is joined with goodness (sattva).
Mahat was born from Saṃkarṣaṇa, and from Pradyumna arose the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra).
Born spontaneously from Aniruddha, I am Brahmā, bearing the form of a crow;
I possess all powers in all things and am endowed with my own supreme power. || 17 ||
The ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), having become threefold, expands all this; namely, the ego-sense as sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa. (18)
The gods are born from the Vaikārika [ego]; the sense organs from the Taijasa; and the elements, beginning with space, from the Tāmasa, each through its own respective power.
Viṣṇu, accompanied by Śrī-Śakti, always protects the three worlds;
Brahmā creates through Bhū-Śakti, and Śiva indeed consumes through Nīla-Śakti.
The Supreme Self shines forth within all living beings;
for all this, O Brahmin, indeed abides within the Supreme Self.
Indeed, in all living beings, two portions always reside;
for the portion that is the individual soul (jīvāṃśa) is predominant, while the portion that is the Supreme Self (paramātmāṃśaka) is indeed [the other].
All the planets beginning with the Sun, as well as Brahmā, Kāma, Dviṣat, and others—these and many more are presided over by portions of the Supreme Self. (23)
And likewise, their powers, such as Śrī and others, are portions of their respective offices;
furthermore, it should be understood that within their various other powers, there are additional portions consisting of individual souls (jīva-aṃśakas). || 24 ||
Now begins the second chapter: On the Narration of the Incarnations.
O Lord of Sages, tell me: are even those incarnations of the Lord of Ramā, such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others, joined with portions of individual souls (jīva)? Or what else is it? Please speak.
O Brahmin, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Nṛsiṃha, and likewise Sūkara—these are indeed complete incarnations (pūrṇāvatāras), while others are endowed with portions of the individual soul (jīvāṃśakas). || 2 ||
Indeed, there are many incarnations of the unborn Supreme Self;
Janārdana, in the form of the planets, bestows the fruits of the karma of living beings. || 3 ||
For the destruction of the strength of the Daityas, for the increase of the strength of the gods,
and for the purpose of establishing righteousness, auspicious [beings] were born from the planets in due order.
Rāma is the incarnation of the Sun; the leader of the Yadus is that of the Moon;
Nṛsiṃha is that of the Son of the Earth (Mars); and Buddha is that of the Son of Soma (Mercury). || 5 ||
Vāmana was the incarnation for the worshiper of the gods (Indra), Bhārgava for Bhārgava,
Kūrma for the son of the Sun (Yama), and Sūkara for Saiṃhikeya (Rāhu).
The Ketu’s incarnation in Pisces and those others which arise from planets—
all those in which the portion of the Supreme Self (Parātmāṃśa) is predominant— are designated as Khecaras.
Those in whom the portion of the individual soul (jīvāṃśa) is predominant are proclaimed as "living beings" (jīva);
they have emerged from the Supreme Self (paramātman), just like the planets beginning with the Sun.
Indeed, all the incarnations, such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others,
always dissolve back into that very [source] once their purpose has been accomplished.
Those [elements] have emerged from the portions of the individual soul, and from them humans and other beings are born;
they too dissolve back into that very same place, for they merge into the unmanifest.
O Brahmin, all this has been told to you regarding that in which everything exists;
even those beings that will come to be are known as such by the knowers of reality.
Without knowledge of that [astronomy/astronomy], no one else can ever understand it;
therefore, it must necessarily be studied, especially by Brāhmaṇas. (12)
That man who, without knowing the scripture, indeed reviles astrology, shall experience the Raurava hell and blindness in another birth. (13)
Now begins the third chapter: On the Nature and Qualities of the Planets.
O Sage, you have out of affection described the descent of the planets;
please, out of compassion, tell us once more about their qualities, essential nature, and so forth.
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall explain the configuration of the lunar mansions and planets;
those numerous luminous orbs which are seen in the sky. (2)
Among those, some are designated as constellations (nakṣatra) and some as planets (graha). Those which bear the names of constellations are fixed in their positions.
Those which constantly seize the lunar mansions as they move are called *grahas* (planets).
The divisions of the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*) consisting of seven hundred and twenty parts are designated by names beginning with Aśvinī.
Its twelve divisions, known as Aries and so forth, are the well-known zodiac signs; the planets, moreover, are known by the names of the Sun and the others.

The rising of the zodiacal signs is the ascendant (lagna); by its power alone, the auspicious and inauspicious results for living beings must be considered through the conjunctions and separations of the planets. //6//
The designations of the clusters of constellations are to be known from the general treatises;
however, according to this [specific] scripture, I shall now declare the results pertaining to the zodiacal signs and insects.

At whatever time and from whichever planet the observed and calculated positions become identical, from that very point the planets should be made precise; O knower, both direction and time are thus rendered precise.
The ascendant must be calculated precisely using the local risings (rāśyudaya) specific to one's own country;
now, first of all, I shall describe the species, forms, and qualities of the planets.
Now, these are the planets in their respective order: the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu. (10)
Among them, the Sun, Saturn, and Mars; the waning Moon, Rāhu, and Ketu are malefic; the remaining planets are benefic; and Mercury is malefic when conjoined with a malefic. (11)

The Sun is said by the wise to be the soul of all and the lord of the day; the Moon is the friend of the night-lotus and the mind; Mars is the principle of goodness (sattva); and Mercury is the bestower of speech. || 12 ||
To the gods, Venus grants the bliss of knowledge and bestows virility;
he was declared by the ancient sages to be the son of Āyā, and he brings misery.
The Sun and the Moon are the two kings; the son of the Earth (Mars) is to be known as the leader;
Mercury is the prince; and Jupiter and Venus are the two ministers.
Preṣyaka, Raviputra, Senā, and Svarbhānuputraka—O Brahmin, one should thus contemplate the Sun and the others in this sequence. (15)
The lord of the day (the Sun) is reddish-dark; the maker of night (the Moon) has a fair-complexioned body.
Mars has limbs that are not too tall and is red; Mercury is likewise dark like dūrvā grass.
O best of the twice-born, the Guru should be known as fair-limbed, Śukra likewise as dark-brown,
and the son of the Sun (Saturn) is known to have a black body.
O twice-born one, Vahni, Ambu, Śikhijā, Viṣṇu, Vidhaujaḥ,
and Śacikā are to be known as the deities of the Sun and the other celestial bodies in their respective order.
O twice-born one, Mercury and Saturn are both eunuchs; Venus and the Moon are females;
and the Sun, Mars, and Jupiter are to be known as males. (19)
O twice-born one, fire, earth, ether, water, and air are, respectively, the constituent principles (tattvas) of the planets beginning with Mars, in their proper order. (20)
O best of the twice-born, Jupiter and Venus are of the Brahmin caste; Mars and the Sun are Kṣatriyas;
O foremost of the twice-born, the Moon and Mercury are of the Vaiśya caste, and Saturn is a Śūdra.
O twice-born one, Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon are of the nature of *sattva*; Mercury and Venus are likewise *rajas*;
and Saturn and Mars are of the nature of *tamas*.

O twice-born one, a man with eyes honey-brown like the sun, square in build, pure, of a bilious (pitta) constitution, intelligent, and having little hair on his head, is a Brāhmaṇa. O twice-born one! 23.
O twice-born one, the Moon has an abundance of wind and phlegm; he is wise, possesses a round body, has auspicious eyes, speaks sweet words, is fickle, and is afflicted by passion. (24)
O twice-born one, Mars is cruel, with blood-red eyes, possessing a restless yet noble form; he is of a bilious temperament, prone to anger, and has a slender waist.
O Brahmin, one of a pitta constitution has an excellent physique and is eloquent; one of a kapha constitution is fond of excessive laughter; and likewise, one of a vāta constitution is wise.
He has a large body, is venerable, and has tawny hair and eyes;
being of a phlegmatic constitution, he is wise and proficient in all the scriptures.
The son of Bhṛgu is happy, of excellent and beautiful form, with lovely eyes;
he is a composer of poetry (Kāvya), characterized by an abundance of phlegm (kapha), has wind (vāyu) as his dominant humor, and possesses curly hair.
O twice-born one, Śauri has a thin and tall body, tawny eyes, and a nature like the wind; he has large teeth, is lazy, lame, and has coarse hair on his head and body.
Smoky in appearance and blue-bodied, he is terrifying even while dwelling in the forest;
wise and of a windy nature, Svarbhānu is equal to that fire.
Bone, blood, marrow, skin, fat, and semen—of these, O twice-born one, the Sun and the other planets are the presiding deities in their respective order. (31)
The Sun and the other [planets] are, respectively, the lords of temples, water, fire-plays and the like, as well as treasuries, beds, and heaps of grain. (32)

O twice-born one, O best of the twice-born, the solstices, moments, days of the week, seasons, months, fortnights, and years of the sun and other planets should be known in their proper order without hesitation. (33)
Pungent, alkaline, bitter, mixed, sweet, sour, and astringent—these should all be known respectively as the tastes of the planets beginning with the Sun. (34)
Mercury and Jupiter are strong in the east; the Sun and Mars are in the south;
Saturn is in the west; and Venus and the Moon are likewise in the north. (35)
Indeed, during the night, the Moon, Mars, and Saturn are strong;
O best of the twice-born, Mercury should always be known as strong during the day, while the remaining planets are strong during the day. (36)
Mars is strong when in the dark fortnight, while Venus is strong when gentle and endowed with vigor;
a benefic planet is strong during the northern solstice, and the other [malefic] during the southern solstice. (37)
The lords of the year, month, day, and hour are likewise strong;
among these, the one beginning with the year is more powerful than the subsequent ones in order of seniority.
The Sun produces large-bodied [beings], while the Son of the Sun (Saturn) produces those who are unfortunate;
the Moon produces those endowed with milk-like qualities, and the Son of the Earth (Mars) produces those characterized by pungency and the like.
O twice-born one, when Jupiter and Mercury occupy a flower-tree [sign], it becomes fruitful; when Saturn occupies it, it becomes fruitless. In this manner, the planets are to be understood. (40)
Rāhu is of the Cāṇḍāla caste, and Ketu is likewise of another caste;
for Śikhin, Svarbhānu, and Mandi, an anthill is said to be their abode. (41)
O twice-born one, the variegated throat of the lord of serpents is the banner of the Sun;
lead is known as that of Rāhu, and sapphire is to be understood as that of Ketu, O best of the twice-born. (42)
O Brahmin, the preceptor’s garment is yellow silk; likewise, that of Bhṛgu is linen.
That of the Sun is red linen, and that of the Moon is white linen, O twice-born one. (43)
For Mercury, it is black linen; for Mars, a red cloth;
for Saturn, O Brahmin, variegated cloth as well as cotton cloth.
The season of Bhṛgu is Ṛtu, and that of Mars and the Sun is Grīṣma;
the rainy season (Varṣā) is to be known as belonging to the Moon, and likewise Autumn (Śarat) to Jupiter.
O twice-born one, Hemanta is to be known as belonging to Guru, while Śiśira belongs to Śani;
Rāhu has eight months, and Ketu has three months, O twice-born one.
Rāhu, Āra (Saturn), and the lame Moon are to be known as the planets of the elements;
the Sun and Venus are the root-planets, while the others are designated as those belonging to Jupiter.
Among the planets, Saturn is old and bestows an increase in lifespan;
O best of the twice-born, he grants many years according to his natural state.
Aries, Taurus, Capricorn, Virgo, Cancer, Pisces, and Libra—these are declared to be the exaltation signs (ucca-rāśi) of the Sun and the other planets, respectively. (49)
Ten, three, eight, seven, fifteen, five, one, and twenty;
the seventh sign from the exaltation is declared to be the fall, by those same degrees. (50)
In Leo, the Sun has five degrees as its exaltation; others say its trine is its own sign.
For the Moon, Taurus is its exaltation at three degrees; others say its trine consists of those same degrees. (51)
In Aries, the twelve degrees of the Sun constitute Mars's trine; others say it is his own sign.
For Mercury, the fifteenth degrees in Virgo are said to be his exaltation.
Then, five degrees are declared as the trine for [the Sun]; others say it is its own sign.
For Jupiter, ten degrees in Sagittarius are its trine; others say it is its own sign. (53)
For Venus, the ninth part of a lunar day (tithi) is its triplicity sign, and the others are its own signs;
for Saturn, twenty parts in Aquarius are its triplicity sign, and the others are its own signs.

From its own trine, the lords of the fourth, second, twelfth, fifth, ninth, eighth, and eleventh houses are friends; those of the sixth, eighth, and third houses are enemies; and those of the remaining houses possess both characteristics. (55)
The lords of the tenth, fourth, seventh, and twelfth houses become mutual friends at that time; however, those situated elsewhere remain enemies. (56)
At that time and by nature, if it is a friend, it is a "super-friend";
if it is a friend in the state of neutrality, it is a "friend"; but if it is equal to an enemy, it is an "enemy. (57)
If [the planets] are equal toward friend and foe, there is enmity; if they are enemies, there is extreme enmity.
Having thus distinguished these, the astrologer should declare the results for the nativity. (58)

In its exaltation, the auspicious result is full; in a trine, it is reduced by one quarter (three-quarters); in its own sign, it is half; and in the house of a friend, it is proclaimed to be merely one quarter. || 59 ||
Half a point is declared for an even sign, and zero for the sign of fall, setting, or an enemy;
likewise, the wise man should declare the opposite results [for the other positions]. (60)
When the Sun is conjoined with one-fourth of the Viśva (thirteen) plus three parts— that is, with sixteen degrees—
it is the great defect named Dhūma, which destroys all undertakings.
Smoke arising from the mandala is pure, yet the *vyatīpāta* yoga here is a source of fault;
when accompanied by Saturn, this *vyatīpāta* and the halo (*pariveṣa*) cause extreme harm.
A halo that has fallen from the disc of the moon or sun is harmful;
likewise, a rainbow that exceeds one-third of the diameter or is augmented by an eighth part is inauspicious, as is a comet-like celestial body.
When Ketu is conjoined with the same zodiacal sign as the Sun, he becomes equal to the Sun;
these are considered non-luminous planets, malefic, and bestowers of evil. (64)
"When these [planets] occupy the positions of the Sun, the Moon, or the Ascendant, there is the destruction of lineage, longevity, and knowledge.
Thus is the status of defects such as *dhūma* and others, as declared by Padmāsana. (65)
The Gulika and other [planetary periods] from Sunday through Saturday are now determined:
having divided the day into eight parts, they should be counted in sequence starting from the lord of the weekday. (66)
The eighth portion shall be Nirīśa, and the ninth portion is known as Gulika.
Having divided the night into eight parts as well, starting from the fifth [portion] after the lord of the weekday: 67.
One should count this as the eighth division; it is proclaimed as Niṣyati.
A twelfth part is called Gulika, and a fifteenth part is designated as Kāla.
The portion of Mars is declared to be death; the portion of Jupiter is Yamaghaṇṭaka;
the portion of Mercury is Ardhapraharaka; these are clearly determined according to their respective countries of origin. (69)
The precise ascendant produced in one's own locality, according to the desired Gulika, is called Gulika;
from that, one should declare the results for the native. (70)

The sign starting from the trikonas of the Sun and others, measured by breaths equal to the degrees and quarters [of the ascendant], from sunrise until the desired time—that sign is indeed the "breath-position" (prāṇapada). || 71 ||
Having converted one's desired time into *pala*s, divide by fifteen; the resulting quotient and remainder represent the [longitude in] signs and so forth.
When the Sun is situated in the two signs of Aries and Taurus, and when Mars is in the ninth or fifth house, [the following applies].
O best of the twice-born, that which is known as the station of the breath (prāṇapada) should clearly be understood as being situated in the ascendant;
furthermore, when the station of the breath is in the second, fifth, or ninth house from the ascendant, it is likewise so.
One should understand that birth is auspicious even if [the planet] is likewise in the eleventh house;
however, if it should be situated in another house, then one should declare the birth to be inauspicious. (74)
Now begins the chapter on the nature of the zodiac signs. 4.
By the omission of the first and last parts of the day-and-night (ahorātra), only the hour (horā) remains;
by the mere knowledge of that, one should declare the fruit of the birth-rite (jātakarma). || 1 ||
Understand from me in due order that the zodiacal signs beginning with Aries are the limbs of Viṣṇu, who is unmanifest in nature, and of Janārdana, who is Time itself.
Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and thereafter Pisces. (3)
Likewise, [the syllables are placed] on the head and face, the two arms, the heart, the chest, the waist, and the bladder;
as well as on the private parts, the pair of thighs, the pair of knees, and the two shanks.
From Aries, the two feet and likewise the head and so forth are to be known in sequence;
they are movable, fixed, and dual-natured; cruel and non-cruel; male and female. (5)
The [signs] beginning with action are of bile, wind, the three elements, and phlegm;
[the horse] is red-colored, large-bodied, four-footed, and strides at night. (6)
The Aries zodiac sign has its domicile in the east, is a kinsman of the king, moves upon mountains, possesses the quality of passion (rajas),
rises from behind, is fiery, and has Mars as its ruler.
The white bull is the lord of Venus; it is long-bodied, four-footed, slow-moving, and strong.
It belongs to the southern quarter, is domestic, and is the ground for merchants. The bull is a sign of ascension by the back. || 8 ||
The head-rising [wind] is a human couple, one with a mace and the other with a lute;
the western wind is an elephant-footed being, strong at night, and belongs to the class of village-dwelling animals.
Samagātra, Haridvarṇa, Mithuna, Budhādhipa, Pāṭala, Vanacārī, and Brāhmaṇa are the powerful [planets] at night. (10)
The sign of Cancer is known to have many legs, a thick body, the quality of sattva, and an affinity for water; it rises from the back and has the moon as its lord. || 11 ||
The lion is presided over by the Sun; it is a being with four feet, a Kṣatriya, and a forest-dweller.
It rises from the head, has a large body, is pale-white, and possesses great strength in the eastern part of the day.

The sign known as Kanyā (Virgo) is of the mountainous region; it possesses strength during the day, has its rising at the head, its culmination in the middle of the body, two feet, and it moves toward the south.
She is the burning of the grain, the Vaiśya woman, multicolored, and the destroyer; she is the maiden joined with darkness, and as a young girl, she is the sovereign of Mercury.
Tula, rising in the head, rich in the strength of heaven, black, and characterized by the quality of rajas, is a western, earth-dwelling, destructive Śūdra with a medium-sized body and two feet. (15)
Then the lord of Venus has a small body, many feet, is a Brahmin, and is bilious;
he is situated in the north (Saumya), is rich in the strength of the day, is tawny-colored, and originates from water and earth.
The scorpion (Vṛścika) has hair on its body, possesses extremely sharp fangs, and is presided over by Mars;
it is a sign rising by the back (pṛṣṭhodayī), and the bow (Dhanus) is presided over by Jupiter and is of the sattvic nature.
Piṅgala is rich in nocturnal vigor; Pāvaka is a twice-born Kṣatriya.
At the beginning he has four feet, and at the end he is four-footed, with symmetrical limbs and bearing a bow.
Stationed in the east, moving upon the earth, and full of splendor, he was created by Brahmā;
as the lord of Monday, he is terrestrial and powerful during the night in the southern quarter.

One with a prominent hump, large-bodied, variegated, and dwelling in forest lands is considered a land-goer at first; however, one that moves in water at the end is regarded as a source of calamity. (20)
Kumbha, Kumbhī, Nara, Babhruvarṇa, Madhyatantu, Dvipāt, Dyuvīrya, Jalamadhyastha, Vātaśīrṣa, Udayin, and Tamas. (21)
The Śūdra is known as the lord of the western region and is presided over by the deity Agni;
the two Pisces, joined at their tail and mouth, constitute the sign of Pisces, which possesses strength during the day.
The aquatic being is rich in the quality of goodness (sattva), self-abiding, and a water-dweller, O twice-born one;
though footless, it possesses a central body, and being situated in the lunar sphere, it rises from both [the sun and moon].
Thus have been declared the qualities of the zodiac signs— Surācārya (Jupiter), Ādhipa (the Lord), and Ceti (Mercury)—
for the sake of both gross and subtle results concerning those consisting of thirty degrees each.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain; listen, O bull among sages:
having thoroughly purified the birth-ascendant, one should purify the conception.
Therefore, O Maitreya, I shall fully explain it;
you must grasp it—the complete knowledge of the conception and all that pertains to the birth-lagna.

Whatever the sign in which a planet is situated, the interval of its slowness (māndya) should be added to the interval between that sign and the ascendant; whatever results from this, expressed in signs and so forth, [is the true longitude]. (27)
The period beginning from the month [of conception] up to that [time of birth] should be known as originating from the *niṣeka* (conception).
Whatever lord of a house is invisible at the time of birth, that [lord] is joined with the degrees traversed by the moon. (28)
At that time, one should calculate the ascendant and subtract it from the body [the natal ascendant] as before;
from that, the auspicious or inauspicious results for the one situated in the womb should especially be declared. (29)
One may declare the auspicious or inauspicious fortune of the parents, as well as their life or death;
thus, by means of the *niṣeka-lagna*, everything should be correctly understood through one's own discernment.
Now begins the chapter on the specific ascendants (viśeṣalagnādhyāya). || 5 ||
Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall explain before you the various ascendants known as Bhāva-horā, Ghaṭī-lagna, and so forth, each individually. (1)
Starting from sunrise, for five ghaṭikās, that very same ascendant remains as the house-ascendant (bhāvalagna) until the time of birth. || 2 ||

Having divided the elapsed [time] in ghaṭīs and so forth by five, the resulting quotient derived from the signs should be added to the heliacal (audayika) Sun; that is the precise ascendant of the house. || 3 ||
Likewise, O twice-born one, from sunrise for a duration of two and a half ghaṭikās, that which passes is called by the name *horā-lagna*. (4)
The elapsed ghaṭīs and so forth, doubled and divided by five, together with the resulting signs and so forth, should be added to the heliacal rising sun; that indeed is the precise horā-lagna.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the conjunctions of the ghaṭīs,
starting from sunrise up to the time of birth in due order.
If a sign, beginning with Aries, passes through the measure of each individual ghaṭikā, that very [period] is called the ghaṭikā-lagna by Nārada and others. (7)

The signs (rāśis) are equal to ghaṭīs, while the degrees (aṃśas) are measured by half-palas (palārdha). This should be added to the solar longitude at sunrise; that indeed is the true ascendant (lagna) in ghaṭīs. || 8 ||
One should separately write out the house-charts for these successive ascendants;
whatever planets are in whichever sign, they should be placed there just as in the chart of the [natal] sign-ascendant.
Now, I shall describe before you the periods (daśās) of the planets known as Varṇadā;
by the mere knowledge of which one may declare the results concerning lifespan and worldly existence.
For those born with an odd ascendant, one should count from Aries (Meṣa) onwards in regular order;
for those born with an even ascendant, one should count from Pisces (Mīna) onwards in reverse order. || 11 ||
The wise person should count from Aries and Pisces up to the birth ascendant;
likewise, having counted up to the hour-ascendant (horā-lagna), one should proceed further from there.

If both [the subject and the example] are similar in terms of their essential nature (*ojas*) and their commonality (*samatva*), then one should apply them as a numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyā*); however, if they are of a different kind (*vaijātya*), one should separate them. || 13 ||
The sign that follows Aries and Pisces is the one that bestows the caste (varṇa).
O bull among the twice-born, listen as I explain the purpose of this:
the period (daśā) that bestows the caste should be determined from the Hora or the Ascendant, whichever possesses strength.
In an odd sign, the *daśā* occurs according to the sequence of the letters from the ascendant; however, in an even sign, it occurs by the reverse sequence of those respective numbers. (15)
If there is a malefic aspect or a malefic conjunction upon the trine of the Varṇada [ascendant],
then his lifespan shall extend only as far as that sign.
Just as life, death, and so forth are determined in the Rudraśūla [chart],
so too are they determined in the Varṇada [chart] when there is a conjunction of malefics in a trine.
O Brahmin, one should consider the results from the sign of the ascendant just as one does from the sign of the varṇada;
from the seventh house from the varṇada, one should consider the lifespan of the wife. (18)
One should know that from the eleventh house of the elder brother, the third of the younger brother, the fifth of the son, and the fourth of the mother, [the results are determined]. (19)
From the ninth state of the father, one should consider life in this way:
indeed, during the powerful period (daśā) of the trident (śūla) sign, there is misfortune (ariṣṭa).
In this manner, the periods (daśās) of the houses beginning with the body (tanu) must be determined;
and as before, the auspicious and inauspicious results for embodied beings are to be known. || 21 ||
The planetary periods (daśās) do not bestow their specific colors upon the zodiac signs;
having established the sign-periods by multiplying them by twelve, one should then declare the sub-periods (antardaśās) in their proper sequence.
Having thus determined the commencement of the sub-periods (antardaśā) and so forth, one should declare the results;
one should also write down the sub-periods according to both the direct and reverse orders.
The ascendant arising at one's own birthplace is here called the "birth-ascendant" (janmalagna);
the same procedure applies everywhere for the houses, decans, and other ascendants. (24)
Now begins the sixteenth chapter, on the group of sixteen.
O Sage, I have heard from you the qualities of the planets as well as those of the zodiac signs;
now I wish to hear about the divisions of the houses—please speak of them out of compassion.
"O Maitreya, listen as I shall fully declare those sixteen classes which Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, has spoken. (2)

The field, the hour (horā), the decan (dreṣkāṇa), the fourth part (turyāṃśa), the seventh part (saptamāṃśaka), the ninth part (navāṃśa), the tenth part (daśamāṃśa), the solar part (sūryāmśa), and the sixteenth part (ṣoḍaśāṃśaka). || 3 ||
Then there is the twentieth part, the forty-fifth part, the thirty-seventh part,
followed by the forty-eighth part, the fifty-second part, and after that, the sixtieth part.
That is the field (*kṣetra*) of that planet; whichever [planet] is the lord of that sign, [it is its field].
For the Sun and the Moon, it is when they are in an odd sign; in an even sign, it is the opposite. (5)
The Pitṛs are proclaimed as the lords of the lunar hora, and the Devas as those of the solar [hora]. Half of a zodiac sign constitutes a hora; twenty-four such horas are traditionally taught.
From Aries onwards, there are two complete cycles of these horas.
The decans (dreṣkāṇas) are derived from one-third of each zodiacal sign, and they are said to be thirty-six in total;
there are three revolutions of these [decans] starting from Aries and so forth in successive order. (7)
O Nārada, for the signs beginning with Aries, the lords of the decanates (dreṣkāṇas) in their respective order are you (Nārada),
Agastya, and Durvāsas.
The lords of the quadrants beginning with one's own asterism are the rulers of the fourth-parts (turyāṃśa) in the signs starting from Aries;
they are Sanaka, Sananda, Kumāra, and Sanātana.
The lords of the seven divisions (saptāṃśa) in odd signs are to be counted from their own ruler, whereas in even signs they are to be known from the lord of the seventh asterism and so forth. 10.
Alkali and milk, curd and clarified butter, as well as that produced from sugarcane juice, honey, pure water, and cow-urine—these are equal [in potency] to pure water and the others. (11)

The lords of the navāṃśas are [determined] from that [sign] in movable signs, from the ninth [counted] from that in fixed signs, and from the fifth [counted] from that in dual signs; thus should it be considered by the wise. Furthermore, gods, humans, and rākṣasas reside in the movable and other houses respectively. (12)
If these [deities] are from one's own [lineage], they are assigned a tenth part; if they belong to the pair [of lineages], they are recorded as being from the ninth.
The ten guardians of the directions beginning with the east are Indra, Agni, Yama, and Rākṣasa.
Varuṇa, Māruta, Kubera, Īśāna, Padmaja, and Ananta— these are to be placed in order, or alternatively, in reverse order.
The calculation of the twelfth part should be determined from each respective field;
their presiding deities, in order, are Gaṇeśa, the Aśvins, and Yama. (15)
The sixteen degrees beginning with Aries, Leo, and Aquarius are to be known as the *cara* (movable) signs and so forth;
in odd signs they are Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, while in even signs the order is reversed. (16)

Now, the lords of the twenty parts as declared by Brahmā are: from Aries, Taurus, and Gemini; from Cancer, Leo, and Virgo; from Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius; and from Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. (17)
Kālī, Gaurī, Lakṣmīvijayā, Vimalā, Satī, Tārā, Jvālāmukhī, Śvetā, Lalitā, and Bagalāmukhī. (18)
One should contemplate Pratyaṅgirā, Śacī, Raudrī, Bhavānī, Varadā, Jayā, Tripurā, and Sumukhī during times of adversity. (19)
In the even zodiac sign (samarāśi), [the goddesses are] Dayā, Medhā, Cinnāśīrṣā, Piśācinī, Dhūmāvatī, Mātaṅgī, Bālā, Bhadrā, Aruṇā, and Analā. 20.
Piṅgalā, Cuccukā, Ghorā, Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, Sitā, Bhuvaneśī, Bhairavī, Maṅgalā, and Aparājitā. || 21 ||
The lords of the Siddha portions are Siṃha and others when the planet occupies an odd sign;
when the planet is in an even sign beginning with Karka, they are Skanda, Parśudhara, and Anala. (22)
Viśvakarman, Bhaga, Mitra, Maya, Antaka, Vṛṣadhvaja,
Govinda, Madana, and Bhīma are to be contemplated in sequence starting from Aries and the other odd signs;
in the even signs starting from Cancer, one should contemplate them in reverse order from Bhīma.

The lords of the lunar mansions (bhāṃśādhipāḥ) are, in order: the Aśvins, Yama, Agni, Pitāmaha (Brahmā), Candra (the Moon), Īśa (Śiva), Aditi, Jīva (Bṛhaspati), Ahi (Sarpa), the Pitṛs, and the one named Bhaga. || 24 ||
Aryaman, Mārka, Tvaṣṭṛ, Marut, Cakra, Agni, Mitra, Vāsava;
Nirṛti, Uda, Viśvedevas, Ajagovinda, Vasus, and Ambupa. (25)
Then Ajapāda, Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan are proclaimed as the lords of the lunar mansions (nakṣatreśas),
who are also the lords of the degrees (bhāṃśeśas) according to the sequence of the four-footed signs beginning with Aries.

In odd signs, the lords of the third-parts (triṃśāṃśa) are Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus; in even signs, they are [Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Venus, and Mars], respectively, by reversing the order of five, five, eight, seven, and six degrees.
Fire, Wind, Indra, Kubera, and likewise Varuṇa are to be known in odd signs respectively; in even signs, the order is reversed. (28)
One should know that for odd signs, the lords of the forty divisions proceed from Aries;
for even signs, they are to be known as proceeding from Libra, each joined with its own respective lord. || 29 ||
Viṣṇu, Candra, Marīci, Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhātṛ, Śiva, Ravi, Yama, Yakṣa, Gandharva, Kāla, and Varuṇa. || 30 ||
Likewise, the lords of the twelve parts of the zodiac are as follows: in a movable sign, they begin from Aries;
in a fixed sign, from Leo; and in a dual sign, from Sagittarius. [The lords of the three periods] are Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu in the movable signs. (31)
O best of the twice-born, the gods Īśa, Acyuta, Surajyeṣṭha, Viṣṇu, and Keśa are to be known as residing in the two fixed signs (Capricorn and Taurus) through fifteen repetitions.
Subtracting the signs from the planet, the resulting degrees and so forth are doubled and divided by twelve;
the remainder increased by one is known as the lord of that sign, with its authority extending over sixty degrees.
Ghora, Rākṣasa, Deva, Kubera, Yakṣa, Kinnara, Bhraṣṭa, Kulaghna, Garala, Vahni, Māyā, and Purīṣaka. (34)
The Lord of Waters, the one accompanied by the Maruts, Time, the serpents, nectar, and the Moon;
the gentle, the soft, Heramba, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (35)
Devārdra, Kalināśa, Kṣitīśakamalākara, Gulika, Mṛtyukāla, and Dāvāgni, who is known as Ghorasaṃjñaka. || 36 ||
Yama, Kaṇṭaka, Sudhāmṛta, Pūrṇaniśākara, Viṣadagdha, Kulānta, and Mukhya Vaṃśakṣaya; || 37 ||
Utpātaka, Kālasaumya, Komala, Śītala, Karāladaṃṣṭra, Candrāsya, Pravīṇa, and Kālapāvaka. (38)
Daṇḍabhṛt, Nirmala, Saumya, Krūra, Atiśītala, Amṛta, Payodhi, Bhramaṇa, and Ākhyau—these are the names of the odd-numbered lunar digits (candrarekhā). || 39 ||

The lords of the sixty-part divisions (ṣaṣṭyaṃśa) are to be known as follows: they are proclaimed to be the same [as the lords of the signs] through transposition in even signs, whereas in odd signs, the lords of the sixty-part divisions are the reverse of those lords. (40)
Planets conjoined with auspicious ṣaṣṭyaṃśas bestow auspicious results;
however, when conjoined with cruel ṣaṣṭyaṃśas, these wanderers of the sky cause destruction. (41)
O Maitreya, I shall declare the divisions of the groups; you must retain them:
the six groups, the seven groups, the ten groups, and the royal groups. (42)
In the combination of groups, there are six groups beginning with Kiṃśuka;
that which consists of two [consonants] is named Kiṃśuka, and that which consists of three is called Vyañjana. (43)
With four [beads] there is that called the chowrie, and with five the parasol;
with six there is the application of the earrings, and with seven that called the crown.
Now, within the group of seven and the group of directions, there are those known by names such as Pārijāta;
Pārijāta is formed with two [syllables], while the Uttama is said to consist of three.
With four [parts] it shall be called Gopura; likewise, with six, Siṃhāsana;
with six, Pārāvata; and with seven, Devaloka.
With eight [letters] there is that called the world of Brahmā; with nine, the vehicle of Śakra; with ten, the union with the abode of Śrī; then, in the group of sixteen: 47.
The *bhedaka* consists of two [syllables], while that called *kusuma* consists of three;
the *nāgapuṣpa* consists of four, and that named *kanduka* consists of five. (48)
That which consists of six [syllables] is called Kerala; with seven, it is Kalpavṛkṣaka;
with eight, Candana; and with nine, Pūrṇacandraka.
By the *dig* [deities] it is named Uccaiḥśravas; by the Rudras it becomes Dhanvantari;
by the Sūryas it becomes Sūryakānta; and by the Viśvedevas it is called Vidruma. (50)
The Śakra-siṃhāsana is formed by the Śakras, and Goloka by the lunar days (tithis); that called Srīvallabha is formed by kings; thus the divisions are declared according to their groups.
The auspicious divisions (vargas) of the lords of one's exaltation, Moolatrikona, and own house, as well as those of the lords of the Kendras from the Arudha Lagna, should be taken by the wise. 52.

Those [planets] that have set, are conquered by other planets, are in their signs of debilitation, or are weak, as well as those situated in the *śayana* (sleeping) and other such positions—[the yogas] produced from them are destroyers of the yoga. (53)
Now begins the seventh chapter: The Analysis of the Vargas.
Now, among the sixteen groups [of houses], I shall explain the distinctions:
the knowledge of the body is in the ascendant (lagna), and prosperity and so forth are in the hour (horā). || 1 ||
In the Dreṣkāṇa, there is happiness arising from brothers; in the fourth ninth-part (turyāṃśa), one considers fortune;
and in the seventh ninth-part, one considers sons, grandsons, and so forth. || 2 ||
In the ninth division (navamāṃśa), there is consideration for one's wives; in the tenth division, great results;
likewise in the twelfth division, and in the sixteenth division, consideration for one's parents.
The knowledge of pleasure and pain, as well as that of vehicles, and the knowledge of worship—this is to be accomplished in the twentieth part. (4)
The strength and weakness of Vidyā are determined by its position in the arms (24°) and the shoulders (12°) of the zodiac;
the result of misfortune occurs within a thirty-degree span, while auspicious and inauspicious effects occur within a forty-degree span. || 5 ||
One should observe everything in the twenty-fourth part (akṣavedāṃśaka) as well as in the sixtieth part (ṣaṣṭyaṃśa).
Wherever the lord of a malefic ṣaṣṭyaṃśa may arrive, [one must take note]. || 6 ||
In this matter, there is no doubt regarding destruction, according to the words of Garga and others:
wherever the auspicious lord of the ninth-part (kalāṃśa) arrives, [there is no harm]. || 7 ||
In that regard, increase and nourishment are according to the words of Garga and others;
thus, the divisions of the sixteen classes have been explained.

Having examined the divisions (vargas) and twentieth-parts (viṃśopakas) of a planet in relation to the states such as its rising and so forth, or its positions in the houses, one should understand their auspicious or inauspicious nature.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the strength of the twenty-fold group, the knowledge of which brings the ripening [of karma] within the range of vision for one who is afflicted. (10)
The twenty-point house-chart (viṃśopaka) of the sky-travelers, beginning with the Sun, should be examined;
their strength is full when they are in their own houses or exaltations, and zero when situated in the seventh house from there. (11)
The lord of two signs should likewise be understood according to the position of the planet;
in the middle, it should be known through proportionate calculation (anupāta), based on the distinction between odd and even asterisms (nakṣatra).
Jupiter, the Sun, and Mars yield the results of the solar hour (sūryahorā), while the Moon, Venus, and Saturn bestow the results of the lunar hour (candrahorā). || 13 ||

The wise man should grant two results when [the Moon] is equal, and the lunar result otherwise; the Sun's result applies from its own hour onwards, while it is devoid of results at the end of the day (virāmaka).

One should consider [the results] everywhere through proportional calculation (anupāta) in the middle; likewise for every decan (dreṣkāṇa), and also for the fourth-parts (turyabhāga) and the ninth-parts (navāṃśa) and so forth, by oneself, as one does for a house.
The Sun bears the results of Mars, and the Moon (the lord of night) bears the results of Venus;
these should be considered within their respective thirty-degree divisions, and here too, it is remembered to be treated like a house.
The ascendant, the horā, the decan (dṛkāṇa), the navāṃśa, the drekāṇa, and the triṃśāṃśa—these six dignities (ṣaḍvarga) here constitute the viṃśopas in their respective order. || 17 ||
In the group of seven, the stages are fifty-one, multiplied by five;
there, the Viśvakas are five with a seventh part, and the eyes are two. (18)
Three, two and a half, four and a half, and two are the leaders of the nights;
having established the gross fruit from each of those, one should then [establish] the subtle.
Ten degrees increased by ten minutes, one-sixtieth of a minute, and three parts of sixty-five—this is to be known as the measure of a sign. (20)
The remaining [planets] are proclaimed to have one-fourth parts plus one and a half;
now I shall specifically describe the strength known as *viṃśopaka*.
Respectively, for the sixteen groups beginning with the *kṣetra*, their *horā*, *triṃśāṃśa*, and *dṛkkāṇa* belong to the Moon, the Crescent Moon, and the Full Moon, respectively. (22)
Two parts of a *kalā* are to be known, and three parts of a *nandā*;
in the *kṣetra*, there are three and a half, while for a *ṣaṣṭyaṃśaka*, there are four.
Half of half [of that] is for the remaining [planets]; this is declared to be their own [maximum].
A full *viṃśopaka* is for Venus; *dhṛti* (twenty) is for Mercury in the case of *adhimitraka* (very friendly).
Fifteen are declared for a friend, ten are proclaimed for a neutral;
for an enemy it is seven, and for a great enemy it shall be twenty-five less a quarter.

The products of the groups, multiplied by their respective universals (viśva) and divided again by twenty, constitute that which is suitable for application as the universal fruit; indeed, it is not fruitful when diminished by five.
Beyond that, it yields very little fruit; beyond ten [yojanas], it is considered middling;
and beyond that, it yields full fruit—this should be understood for all those who move through the sky.
Now, O Maitreya, I shall tell you something else; listen attentively.
White [planets], situated in the seventh house from the Sun, bestow a full fruit. (28)

One should understand the absence of results when the Sun and the planet are in the same sign; for everywhere, the twenty-point (viṃśopaka) values for rising and setting are determined through proportional calculation in the middle.
O bull among the twice-born, the result of this should be known as a twentieth part of the group;
having understood whatever result pertains to whichever [factor], that result has been proclaimed.
First, there is the twenty-part division (vargaviṃśopaka); thereafter, from sunrise until sunset, one should always contemplate that which is full as being "fuller than full" (pūrṇetipūrṇa). || 31 ||
That which is inferior is called "inferior" (hīna), and it is remembered as being very small, small, or extremely small;
that which is middling is called "middling" (madhya), lasting as long as its ten-fold state persists. (32)
Now, O Maitreya of noble vows, I shall speak of something else; listen well.
The fourth, seventh, and tenth houses from the ascendant are specifically designated as *kendras* (angular houses). (33)
O twice-born one, it should be known that the second, fifth, and ninth houses are called *paṇaphara*,
while the third, sixth, eleventh, and twelfth houses are called *āpoklima*.
The fifth and ninth houses from the ascendant are designated as *koṇa* (angles).
The sixth, eighth, and twelfth houses are designated as *duḥ* (troublesome) and are also known as *trika* (triplicities). || 35 ||
O best of the twice-born, they say that the fourth opening is square;
for from one's own position, the houses of gain are the third, sixth, eleventh, and tenth. (36)
The body, wealth, siblings, kinsmen, sons, and enemies; likewise, women, the void (the ninth house), dharma, action, gain, and expenditure follow in order. (37)
This has been stated briefly; other matters may be understood according to one's own intelligence.
I shall, however, mention some specific details as they were uttered from the mouth of Brahmā. 38.

Whatever knowledge exists in the ninth house from the father, or in the ninth from the Sun, or whatever exists in the tenth or the eleventh house, that is to be understood from the tenth house from the Sun. (39)
Whatever is contemplated in the fourth, body, second, eleventh, or ninth houses from the Sun, one should certainly contemplate that in the fourth, body, eleventh, or ninth houses from the Moon. (40)

Whatever [is to be considered] regarding the third house from the Ascendant and the entirety [of the matter] regarding the tenth house from Mars, one should examine the sixth house from Mercury. || 41 ||
[The results are determined] from the son's [ascendant], from the son of the guru, from the wife, from the seventh house from Bhrigu (Venus), from the eighth, and also from the twelfth;
likewise from Saturn in the eighth or the twelfth.
Whatever fruit is to be considered as arising from a particular state, the wise know that fruit to come from Īśa;
for that fruit of His is indeed what must be contemplated therein as either auspicious or inauspicious.
Now begins the eighth chapter, concerning the description of planetary aspects upon signs.

Now, O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall explain separately the various aspects of the aspectual vision (dṛṣṭi) of the zodiac signs beginning with Aries, categorized by their movement (cara) and other qualities. || 1 ||
O Brahmin, the signs facing [the observer] see those on their sides in the same way;
just as a movable sign sees the immovable ones, so indeed does an immovable sign see the movable ones.
Devoid of its own self-nature, it perceives things of dual nature;
likewise, the planets have departed from that place, leaving behind what was near at hand.
Planets situated in movable signs aspect those joined with fixed signs;
likewise, those situated in fixed signs aspect those situated in movable signs. (4)
The planets beginning with the Sun, situated in both [the zodiacal signs], see those situated in both;
this is the traditional teaching that planets do not see one another when they are in close proximity.
I shall describe the wheel of views exactly as it was proclaimed by Brahmā;
by its mere arrangement, the various distinctions of view are revealed.
O Brahmin, Cancer and Leo are to be drawn in the east; likewise, Libra and Scorpio in the north;
and Capricorn and Aquarius in the south.
One should draw a couple in the northeast corner, a maiden in the northwest,
a bow in the southwest, and a staff in the southeast corner.
Having thus properly arranged the wheel of vision (dṛṣṭicakra) in either a four-armed form or a circular form, one should then investigate the vision.
Now begins the chapter on fatal signs (ariṣṭa). || 9 ||

O Brahmin, at the outset one should examine the auspicious and inauspicious signs (ariṣṭa) pertaining to birth from the limbs [of the body]; thereafter, one should declare the results of the horoscope (jātaka) for the houses beginning with the ascendant (tanu). || 1 ||
For as long as twenty-four years pass from birth, there may be danger to life from birth itself; during that time, one should not consider the span of one's life.
The Moon situated in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth house, aspected by malefic planets, brings death immediately to the newborn; however, if it is aspected by benefics, death occurs after eight years.

If the benefics are like the moon [in aspect] yet give death, and are retrograde or aspected by malefics, then for a child born when the ascendant is devoid of benefics, death occurs within a month. (4)
If the Sun, Saturn, Moon, Mars, and Jupiter should reside in the intellect (the fifth house) at the time of one's birth,
then both his mother and his brother will swiftly meet their end.
Mars, aspected by malefics and conjoined [with them], situated in the ascendant and unaspected by benefics, bestows death;
likewise, even when placed in the eighth house, he does so if conjoined with Saturn or the Sun.
If Rāhu is conjoined with the Moon or the Sun during a lunar or solar eclipse,
and the ascendant is aspected by Saturn and Mars, he lives for one fortnight.
Saturn situated in the tenth house, the moon in the sixth house,
and Mars in the seventh house— one perishes along with one's mother.
If the son of the Sun (Saturn) is in the ascendant and the Moon is in the eighth house,
and Jupiter is situated in the third house, that person goes to the abode of Yama.
If the Sun is in the ninth house of the Hora, Saturn is situated in the seventh,
Jupiter is in the eleventh, and Venus [is present], he lives for one month.
In the twelfth house, all planets are unfavorable; however, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, and Rāhu are particularly destroyers, causing ruin either through their aspect or by their presence.
If the Moon, joined with malefic planets, is situated in the ninth house or the seventh or the ascendant,
and is aspected by or conjoined with malefics, it then brings death to the infant.
Indeed, during the twilight, the lunar hour (horā), or the Gaṇḍānta, it leads to death;
furthermore, destruction occurs when the Moon and malefic planets are each situated in the angles (kendras). || 13 ||
The evening twilight (saṃdhyā) lasts for three nāḍīs from half the setting of the sun;
likewise, the morning twilight lasts for three nāḍīs prior to half the rising [of the sun]. (14)

If malefic or benefic planets are situated in the first or seventh halves of the zodiacal signs beginning with Cancer (the Crab), and the ascendant is in a sign of a fixed nature (kīṭabha), one goes to one's death; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
If malefic planets are situated in the twelfth, sixth, or eighth houses, or likewise in the second house, and the ascendant is situated between malefic planets, one should truly predict death. (16)
When malefic planets occupy the ascendant and the seventh house, and the Moon is also conjoined with a cruel planet, yet is not aspected by benefic planets, then death will occur swiftly. (17)

O Lord of Brahmins, he who is born when the waning moon is situated in the ascendant and malefic planets are positioned in the angles (kendras) and the eighth house, meets with death; of this there is no doubt.
If the Moon is situated between two malefic planets, or occupies the ascendant, the eighth, the twelfth, or the seventh house, that infant who is born at such a time will meet death before long. (19)
When the Moon is situated between two malefics and occupies the ascendant,
and there is a malefic in the seventh or eighth house, the infant dies along with its mother.
One who is born when Saturn, the Sun, and Mars are situated in the twelfth, ninth, and eighth houses,
and are aspected by Śani and Bhairava, has gone to his death.
If a malefic planet is situated in the decanate (dreṣkāṇa) or the inimical sign of anyone,
and the waning moon is positioned in the ascendant, it instantly takes away that person's life.
All planets situated in their fall (āpoklima) are devoid of strength;
his lifespan is declared to be either six months or two months.
If the Moon is aspected by three malefic planets at birth, there will be the destruction of his mother; however, if it is aspected by benefics, one should predict auspiciousness. || 24 ||
When Rāhu, Mercury, Venus, Saturn, or the Sun is situated in the second house (Dhana), death shall occur to his mother; this happens when the father has died. || 25 ||

If the Moon is situated in the seventh house from the Ascendant or the eighth house from the Moon, conjoined with malefic planets, and aspected by strong malefics, the person born becomes a slayer of his mother. (26)
Whether the Sun is situated in its exaltation, its fall, or in the seventh house, the child shall be deprived of drink; he lives only on goat's milk. (27)
When a malefic planet situated in the fourth house from the Moon is in an inimical sign, it causes the death of the mother, provided there is no benefic in a quadrant. (28)

When a malefic planet is situated in the twelfth house as well as the sixth house, one should know there is danger for the mother; likewise, if it is in the fourth and tenth houses, there is danger for the father. (29)
If a malefic planet is in the ascendant, a malefic in the twelfth house, and likewise a benefic in the second house,
yet a malefic is in the seventh house, it causes the destruction of one's retinue.
If Jupiter is situated in the ascendant, Saturn in the second house, and Rāhu in the third house at the time of birth, his mother does not live.
If malefic planets, devoid of benefics, occupy the trines from the waning Moon,
the mother will undoubtedly abandon her life within six months.
When the two Mandāra planets are situated in one sign, wherever that may be,
or when they both occupy the Moon's sign or its quadrant, one does not live past two mothers.
If Mars is in the seventh house from the ascendant and the Moon is in the sixth house at the time of birth, his father does not live.
If Jupiter is in the ascendant and Saturn, Venus, Mars, and Mercury are in the second house at the time of the boy's marriage, his father dies.
If the Sun is conjoined with a malefic planet, or situated between two malefics, and a malefic is located in the seventh house from the Sun, then there shall be the death of one's father. (36)
If the Sun, the delighter of the earth, is situated in the seventh house in the tenth house of action,
and Rāhu is in the twelfth house of that same person, his father lives with great hardship.
When Mars is situated in the tenth house and has entered the sign of an enemy, the father of that person born will die quickly; of this there is no doubt. (38)
When the Moon is in the sixth house, Saturn is in the ascendant,
and Mars is in the seventh house, his father does not live.
When the Sun is situated in the Bhauma-aṃśaka and is aspected by Saturn,
there will be the cessation of [the effects of] a previous birth, or else the death of the infant or its father.
When two malefic planets are situated in the fourth, the tenth, and the twelfth houses,
one goes from country to another country after having killed one's father and mother.
If Rāhu and Jupiter are in an enemy's sign in the ascendant or in the fourth house,
in the twenty-third year, the son does not see his father.
The Sun is the father of all living beings, and the Moon is likewise their mother;
yet the Sun, when conjoined with malefic aspects or situated between malefic planets, [causes harm].
One should certainly recognize the misfortune of the father for a newborn child if malefic planets,
devoid of benefic ones, are situated in the sixth or eighth asterisms from the Sun,
or even if they are located in the house of happiness (the fourth house). || 44 ||
Thus, one should determine the suffering of the mother from the malefic planets situated from the Moon; or, by discerning their strength and weakness, one should predict suffering or death. (45)
Now begins the tenth chapter: On the Destruction of Misfortune (Ariṣṭabhaṅga).
Thus have I declared the *ariṣṭas* (signs of death), and their cancellation is now being told;
having observed these, a wise man should declare whether there is danger or safety for those born. || 1 ||
If even a single Jñānārī or Śukra is situated in a quadrant from the ascendant,
it destroys all misfortune, just as the sun destroys darkness.
A single powerful living soul situated in the ascendant destroys the accumulation of misfortunes,
just as a prostration performed with devotion destroys sin for the wielder of the trident.
If the lord of the ascendant alone is situated in a quadrant and endowed with strength,
he destroys all misfortune, just as the wielder of the Pināka bow destroyed Tripura.
If birth occurs at night during the bright fortnight under an auspicious ascendant aspected by benefic planets, it destroys misfortune; the opposite is true for the dark fortnight. || 5 ||
When the Sun is in the twelfth house at the time of birth in the sign of Libra, that child shall live for a hundred years and become long-lived. (6)
When Jupiter and Mars are conjoined, or when Mars is aspected by Jupiter,
it destroys all misfortune pertaining to the mother and brings about auspiciousness.
When a malefic planet is situated between two benefics in the fourth or tenth house,
it forms a yoga that brings happiness to one's father, provided the benefic planets occupy the quadrants or the trines.

When malefic planets are situated within the benefic [Navāṃśas] and benefics are placed in the angles (kendras) and trines (trikoṇas), they immediately destroy misfortune; however, that does not negate the results arising from the specific house concerned.
The End of India
